archival_memory.user_cs_class_connections: I made plenty of connections through my computer science classes—study groups, group projects, or just the random folks I always saw in the lab at two in the morning, trying to debug code the night before a big assignment. There's this sense of solidarity that comes from those late-night coding sessions—like we're going through the trenches together.
archival_memory.user_cs_class_friends: I vividly remember this one time in my sophomore year, there was a particularly infamously difficult systems programming course. Our final project was basically building a mini operating system kernel from scratch, and we were all losing our minds with memory management bugs. That's actually how I became tight with Carla, another CS major. We ended up bonding over pizza at 3 a.m. because we were the only two left in the lab so late. Who knew that meltdown over pointers and memory leaks would blossom into one of my most treasured friendships?
archival_memory.user_gym_friends: I kept seeing the same group of people in the early mornings at the gym, and it kind of turned into this friendly circle. One of those guys, Dean, is a fellow computer science major, but he's more into machine learning and hardware acceleration projects. We started talking shop between sets, which led to us comparing notes on our classes, which then led to us being gym buddies who share nutritional tips, workout regimens—pretty much everything. Now, every so often, we'll game together, too. He's the one who got me hooked on a new co-op adventure game, so it's not just about the gym lifts anymore. It's become a friendship built around mutual support—pushing each other to be better in multiple areas of life.
archival_memory.user_gym_friends_benefits: I've found a supportive community at the gym, where I can blow off steam and stay motivated. archival_memory.user_library_friends: I've bumped into the same faces in the same corner desks at the campus library over the years. One of those people is Jackson, a law student who was reading case studies right next to my stack of cryptography textbooks. We started chatting during water breaks, comparing our respective workloads. Over time, we realized we shared an interest in debates—oddly enough, he loves analyzing political and ethical implications of new technologies, so I'd talk to him all day about algorithmic bias. We discovered that, even though we come from different disciplines, we both care about how technology intersects with society's legal structures. Our friendship is more intellectual than some of my others, but it's one I truly value because it broadens my perspective beyond code and servers.

archival_memory.user_transcending_distance: I think real friendship is about having a strong sense of trust, loyalty, and empathy that can transcend distance. I've seen that in Tony, who's interning across the country this semester, yet we still FaceTime regularly. I see the same dedication in others, like Carla, who's applying to master's programs abroad. We promised that if either of us ends up in Europe, the other has to come visit. It's amazing how these bonds can endure despite physical distance.

archival_memory.user_gratitude: I'm extremely grateful for the friendships I've made through sailing, the gym, gaming, research, random campus encounters—everything. They're truly an integral part of my college experience, and they remind me that there's more to this journey than racking up achievements on my resume. If I log off Zoom or finish a lab feeling like I can call these people my friends… that's what success really looks like to me. And I know that no matter where I end up in my career, I'll carry a piece of each of these friends with me. Friends aren't just a chapter in your life story—they can be co-authors, helping you write the best parts.
